newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Maskhadov vows to make Chechnya fully independent.
newsitem.headline: Maskhadov vows to make Chechnya fully independent.

text.p: Guerrilla chief Aslan Maskhadov claimed victory on Tuesday in Chechnya's presidential election and vowed to turn the tiny mountainous region into an internationally recognised sovereign state.

"The whole Chechen people, after these two years, have been waiting for this day and have placed many hopes in this day. I'm very glad that...the people have made the right choice," Maskhadov told a news conference in the Chechen capital Grozny.
Surrounded by camouflage-clad field commanders, Maskhadov -- who aides say captured about 58 percent of the vote in Monday's poll -- said Chechnya's political status was already fixed.

"We determined in 1991 that Chechnya was an independent state and declared sovereignty. All that remains is for other countries, including Russia, to recognise that. This can be achieved by political means," he said.
The softly spoken Maskhadov, who wore a leather jacket and traditional lambswool hat, added he would not settle for less.
Under last August's peace deal, the Kremlin, which wants to keep Chechnya within the Russian Federation, and the rebels agreed to defer the region's final political status for five years.
But Maskhadov, a former Soviet artillery colonel who led the guerrilla army and then headed the peace talks, said he was ready to reopen negotiations on Chechnya's status immediately.
"We're ready, even tomorrow, the day after, any time," he said. "The sooner the better. It all depends on Russia."
Maskhadov's running mate for the post of vice-president struck an even more uncompromising note in comments made to Russia's NTV commercial television.
"Russia has always been letting us down, Russia has never kept its word," said Vakha Arsanov. "We won't live as part of Russia. The world should know about this."

Maskhadov, regarded as the most pragmatic presidential candidate by Moscow despite his pro-independence line, told reporters he regreted what he called a strong anti-Chechen tone among Russian politicians and mass media.
"To my great regret, it seems Russia is not ready for a sensible approach to establishing mutually beneficial relations with us. We are offering a sensible approach," he said.
In Moscow President Boris Yeltsin cautiously welcomed Maskhadov's likely victory and senior aides met to plot Russian strategy towards the breakaway region.
But Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky reiterated Russia's opposition to outright Chechen independence.
Maskhadov, 45, said he would seek reparations from Russia for the devastation his region had suffered during the war.
"Our economic situation is woeful...Nearly everything has been destroyed," he said, adding that Chechens must develop "internal resources" like agriculture.
But returning to a key theme of his election campaign, Maskhadov said ethnic Russians still living in Chechnya had a role to play in the region's future and should stay.

He also said he hoped to offer a government post to his runner-up in the election, hardline field commander Shamil Basayev. Earlier he had chided Basayev, regarded in Russia as a terrorist, for running a dirty campaign.
